\chapter*{Devanagari for Marathi --- a reference}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{Devanagari for Marathi (reference)}
\markboth{Devanagari}{Devanagari}

A \textbf{reference}, not a chapter — the lessons teach reading through real words. This page gathers the system and flags what is special about \emph{Marathi's} Devanagari.

\section*{How Devanagari works (the three facts)}

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item \textbf{Consonants carry a built-in \textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{}.} \mr{क} = ka, \mr{न} = na, \mr{म} = ma.
  \item \textbf{A vowel sign (\emph{mātrā}) changes it:} \mr{का} kā · \mr{कि} ki · \mr{की} kī · \mr{कु} ku · \mr{के} ke · \mr{को} ko · \mr{कौ} kau.
  \item \textbf{A \emph{halant} removes it}, and the bare consonant joins the next as a conjunct: \mr{स्} + \mr{का} $\to$ \mr{स्का}; \mr{न्} + \mr{य} $\to$ \mr{न्य}. The \emph{anusvāra} dot \mr{ं} nasalises a vowel (\mr{बरं} \emph{baraṃ}).
\end{enumerate}

\section*{What is special about Marathi's Devanagari}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item \textbf{The extra letter \mr{ळ} (\emph{ḷa})} — a \textbf{retroflex l}, tongue curled back. Hindi does \emph{not} have it; Marathi shares it with the Dravidian languages to the south — Tamil, Kannada and the rest — a mark of centuries of contact. Common in \emph{kāḷ} (\textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{}), \emph{phaḷ} (\textquotedblleft{}fruit\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{The vowel \mr{ॲ} / \mr{ऍ}} for the English \textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{} of \emph{cat} — added for English loanwords (\emph{bĕnk}, \textquotedblleft{}bank\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{Three genders.} Marathi keeps Sanskrit's masculine, feminine, \emph{and} neuter (Hindi collapsed to two), and marks gender on verbs and adjectives more thoroughly — even in the present tense (\emph{yeto} m. / \emph{yete} f.).
\end{itemize}

\section*{Marathi in the family}

Marathi is \textbf{Indo-Aryan} (like Hindi, Punjabi, Bengali — descended from Sanskrit), spoken in Maharashtra. Its script and much formal vocabulary are shared with Hindi and Sanskrit; its sound system, the letter \mr{ळ}, and parts of its grammar bear the imprint of long contact with Dravidian. The lessons trace both threads.
